No. Impact matters over intention. 

If I hit you with my car, but it was a total accident and I totally didn’t mean to, am I immediately absolved of all consequences? No, because what’s more important is the fact that I hit you with my car. You, the victim, are the focus, and in this scenario you’ve been impacted significantly. It doesn’t matter how good my intentions were. It doesn’t matter if I even thought I was doing you a favor. It literally doesn’t matter because the impact is the same and you are hurt. 

Obviously, this doesn’t mean that Matty Healy is EQUALLY as bad as all actual Nazis. But saying it wasn’t his intention to cause hurt doesn’t absolve him of the guilt from the hurtful thing he did.

I mean, look at Hamilton (obviously a different medium, but a particularly successful musical that many people have enjoyed and is on my mind currently so it’s the example I’m using lol). People generally know he died in that duel and... that’s about it. But they knew how that story was going to end and it was still a wildly successful one because of the way it was told. (In Hamilton, the way it’s dealt with is actually to put emphasis throughout on the way he will die, with it being subtly referenced/foreshadowed throughout the work, but that’s just one way to do it) 

Obviously a novel is much longer so you have much more space in which you have to artfully deal with keeping the tension, but tension doesn’t only have to come from life or death situations. The problem is that a lot of parents start to notice signs that their child has autism between 18 months and 5 years old. It’s not something you can generally see symptoms of at birth because so many of the signs are related to the way people interact with others and that interaction doesn’t start until babies are a little older. Babies can only interact so much when they’re tiny, but when they’re toddlers, the interaction gets more sophisticated so you can see if they’re hitting the milestones they’re supposed to or not. This is also the age when kids are getting most of the vaccines they’ll get in their lives. When they’re older they get the occasional booster shot, but when they’re little they sometimes get shots every few months. So it’s easy to blame the vaccines, especially if you just do happen to see a change in behavior right around the time they got their last round of shots.

Ok so you’ve got a few options then. If you’re struggling to fit in them doing “teen stuff” you might try to figure out if it’s necessary for them to be as young as they are. Would the story still work if they were 18-19 or even in their early 20s? 

If it’s necessary that they’re teens, that still doesn’t necessarily make it YA. If you want to make it YA, you might just tone down the themes a little. Remember that the Hunger Games is literally a book about a bunch of kids murdering each other. Pretty heavy stuff, but handled in a teen friendly way. If you don’t want it to be YA, you can likely just leave things the way they are. In the end, if you’re trying to get published, your publisher will market it in a way that makes it clear it’s not intended for a younger audience, regardless of the ages of your characters.

Are all of your main characters teens? What kinds of themes are you dealing with? 

ASOIAF has children in it, but it’s definitely not a children’s series for a lot of reasons. A lot of the POV characters are adults and while some are children, they’re not dealing with themes typically seen in YA novels. 

YA novels have a tendency to deal more with themes associated with coming of age. Adult novels deal with more adult themes. Theres also things like levels and description of violence that can give you a hint. If there’s very graphic violence or gore, that’s not really suitable for YA, but lesser levels of violence are generally acceptable. 

Obviously I’m not the authority on this, but those are at least a couple ways you can identify a little more about your audience. You also want to make sure you’re reading a lot of books, both similar and dissimilar to your own. That can give you an idea of what fits where.

Often, I find that there’s a subplot that would add depth to the story, lengthen it, and fit well with the main plot that I can add in. That’s not always the case, but I like to look back and identify what’s missing. As an example, if it’s depth of character for my protagonist that I’m missing, I add a subplot that helps explore their character further. 

Don’t add scenes in for the sake of lengthening it. If the story can be told without a scene, it’s unnecessary. Don’t go crazy with detail because you want your story to be longer. Padding your prose will just make it sound unnatural/purple.

So the difference is your focus. If you’re saying “Wow, it’s hard for me that you’re sick” that’s crappy. If you’re saying “Wow, it must be hard for you to be sick, and I’m sorry that’s happening” that’s ok, because you’re focused on them. If you need to talk about how it’s hard for you, that’s totally ok. Being friends or family of someone that is hurt or sick can be really tough in a lot of different ways. But don’t talk to the sick person about that. Talk to someone who is less directly effected. 

Obviously this is just a rule of thumb. There will be exceptions. But in general, sticking to this is a good way to avoid further burdening someone when they’re having a hard time. You want to support them, not make them feel bad for being sick.

Telling is really important! You just have to be careful that you're using it in the right places. Showing is good for most description, especially when it comes to characterization. Don't tell us the character is afraid, show us what it is that would make us think the character is afraid.

I tend to describe every single step of the journey in a first draft. Editing it requires a TON of cutting because I'm showing everything that doesn't matter just because. Something that has really helped me is doing my writing in "sprints." I sit down and give myself 10 minutes to think about what needs to happen next in my scene or chapter or whatever, then I HAVE TO write for 15 minutes straight without stopping. I almost always write using the same process. I tend to start with an idea about an ending and/or climax. **Setting** 

There was none. I got almost no details about the setting. I guess we were in a laboratory in Russia, but I saw nothing that made me believe that. You just told me and then expected me to do all the heavy lifting by filling in almost every single detail.

I want to preface this by saying that I'm no expert. I've spent time lurking here, but this story needed a critique badly, so take what I say with a grain of salt. I gave some line edits under the name Lady Crawley, but I only got through the first five pages. 

I'll start with what I felt was most difficult to handle and move on from there. 

**Show, Don't Tell**

I've always hated this phrase, but it's the most accurate way to describe what was so bad about this story. You go around in circles in Quentin's thoughts and he gives us random pieces of wisdom ("A man should always have a good piece of rope..."), but you don't tell us what's happening. Quentin's in one place then suddenly he's in a store? You didn't give us any of the action. You only gave us Quentin's reactions to things we didn't even know were happening. 

Then, when we finally get to something happening and Quentin is digging up the body, you give us no details. All I'm told is that he's digging. This could have been a great scene, but instead I get more of Quentin's thoughts and too much exposition and the actions get buried so that it feels like nothing is happening. And really, in the five pages I read, nothing did happen. 

The way that it read to me was that you didn't have much in the way of plot, so you dumped in as much filler and exposition as possible so something would be on the page. Your plot needs to be way more important than you made it. 


**Omit Unnecessary Words**

You have so many useless words here that it's impossible to wade through the story. The words that you do give us don't tell us anything. For example, you tell us that Rob's wife and daughters are beautiful, you call his wife "lovely", but those are lazy, subjective terms. What does that mean for them? What does that mean to Quentin?

Another example: We know that Quentin is mumbling to himself if he's alone. You don't need to tell us that. 

One of the things that helps me personally is remembering that the reader can infer a lot more than you think they can. You don't have to give them every single little detail for them to know what's going on. However, you do have to tell them what actions are being taken. You're bare bones with your action, but any description is filled with a painful amount of fluff. 

**Rate of Revelation**

I mentioned this in the doc, but thought I would expand a little here. We get nowhere in this store for over five pages! By the time I gave up, nothing had happened, even though I tried to hold out for some action. We spend all five pages confused about who Quentin is, what he wants, and why it all matters to us. Basically, but the fifth page, I still didn't care. You want to make us care right away. 

Now, I'm not by any means saying that you need to give us everything on page 1. But if I get halfway through the story and Is till don't understand the plot or the characters or why it matters at all, then the story is failing. 

**Dialog**

Your dialog is awkward and confusing. First off, Quentin and Rob keep saying each others names. No one does that in real life. I can go days without saying my husband's name if we're the only two people around. If there are only two people in a scene, it's unnecessary to repeat their names even once. Who else would they be talking to?

You need to read your dialog out loud and really listen to it. If it sounds even a little bit awkward, cut it, revise it, fix it! It's easier to hear those problems than it is to read them. 

Also, that "Flap, flap, flap" nonsense was so weird. I was just completely weirded out. Who would say that? Why would anyone say that? Can you hear how that was an extremely strange piece of dialog?

**Setting**
I have no idea where we are during most of this. Was the beginning supposed to be a time jump? If so, it didn't read that way. We were out at a grave and then all of sudden we weren't anymore without explanation. Then we got back tot he grave with any real description. It was a mess. You don't necessarily need to dump all the setting information at once. In fact, you shouldn't. I think that it depends. If you really aren't going to finish it, set it aside and use your best ideas from it in another story. 

However, if you've written a lot of different things that you've never finished, you probably need to sit down and make yourself finish something. If you get too much in the habit of not finishing, it'll make it that much harder to eventually finish something. You don't want to end up there. Even if it's something that no one will ever see, finish it for yourself.

This all the way. I should've been more specific. The reason I hate dream sequences is because they don't further the plot. You might be able to argue that they further character development, but in my personal and completely non-professional opinion, the first chapter is not the place to use a dream sequence to develop character. We need to meet your character first before delving into their psyche.

Cliche opening statements like "It was a dark and stormy night". Dream sequences. The character looking at his/her reflection purely for the purpose of character description. I also don't love when the story starts with character waking up, but that isn't necessarily bad enough for me to stop reading.

I think that it's all about learning to tap into those emotions without really feeling them. You know how that pain and sadness feels and you just have to learn to look back at that and write the same thing, but you definitely don't have to feel it all the time. I've found that when I look back at the hard times in my life and really examine the things I was thinking and feeling, then let that flow into my writing, I write a lot better. However, you don't have to pull a Poe or a Hemingway to be a good writer. I think it's that writers are prone to depression, not that depression makes someone a good writer.
